queue.tree_name: The Horse Chestnut of Square Rene-Le Gall
queue.recognise: Near the garden's obelisk, at one of the entrances.
queue.story:
There is a river under this garden. The Bievre ran through the Gobelins quarter in the open until the city buried the last stretches of it, fouled by the tanners and dyers who had worked its banks for centuries, and Square Rene-Le Gall was laid out in the 1930s across the ground it used to flow over. This horse chestnut was planted in 1893 or 1894, while the water was still above ground.

It stands near the garden's obelisk, at one of the entrances, and its measurements are a small lesson in how slowly a mature tree changes. queue.tree_name: The Dragon Tree of Quinta Conde dos Arcos
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a crown nearly 14 metres across on a trunk barely 6.2 metres tall, wider than it is high. It stands in the Quinta Conde dos Arcos park in Olivais, near the old palace.
queue.story:
This dragon tree is more than twice as wide as it is tall: 6.2 metres of height under a crown almost 14 metres across, on a trunk 4.75 metres round. Dracaena draco grows that way on purpose. It puts up a stem, flowers, then forks, over and over, until an old one looks like an umbrella made of umbrellas.

Nobody can date it properly. Dragon trees lay down no annual rings, so every age published for one is worked back from the branching or from records. The register recorded 200 years when it was measured in 2010, which makes it roughly 215 now, and that is about as precise as this species allows.

It grows in the Quinta Conde dos Arcos, a private estate the Lisbon council expropriated in 1940
queue.name: The Dragon Tree of Quinta Conde dos Arcos
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better
